title: “SELL EVERYTHING YOU HAVE” — DOES JESUS REQUIRE EVERY CHRISTIAN TO BECOME POOR?
paragraphs:
“SELL EVERYTHING YOU HAVE” — DOES JESUS REQUIRE EVERY CHRISTIAN TO BECOME POOR?
The Rich Young Ruler Thought He Owned His Wealth. Then Jesus Exposed the Terrifying Possibility That His Wealth Owned Him.
What if Jesus looked at your bank account, your house, your savings, your business, your retirement fund, your favorite possessions—and then looked directly into your eyes and said:
Because a wealthy man once stood face-to-face with Jesus Christ believing he was ready for eternal life.
And then Jesus touched the one thing the man could not imagine surrendering.
Suddenly, the conversation stopped being theological.
And perhaps that is why this passage still makes Christians uncomfortable two thousand years later.
“One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor…”
He wasn’t talking to an atheist.
He was talking to a man who wanted eternal life.
And the story ends with one of the saddest departures in the Gospels.
The man walked away from Jesus.
Not because he had committed some spectacular public scandal.
He walked away because following Jesus had suddenly become more expensive than he expected.
And before we explain what Jesus meant, there is something even more devastating in the original account that we cannot afford to miss.
ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν
emblepsas autō ho Iēsous ēgapēsen auton
Jesus loved him before giving him the command that hurt him.
This was not a cruel Messiah trying to humiliate a wealthy man.
Jesus saw what everyone else could not see.
People could see the man’s morality.
And sometimes the most loving thing Christ can do is expose the thing we secretly love more than Him.
That is where this passage becomes dangerous.
Because you can spend your entire life asking:
“Does Jesus literally require every Christian to sell everything?”
while avoiding the question the passage is pressing into your heart:
What could Jesus ask you to surrender that would make you walk away sad?
The story appears in Matthew 19:16–30, Mark 10:17–31, and Luke 18:18–30. Mark tells us the man ran to Jesus and knelt before Him.
“Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?”
Jesus eventually directed him toward the commandments.
“Master, all these have I observed from my youth.”
Imagine saying that while standing before the Son of God.
Yet Jesus did not begin arguing with him.
Then pierced directly through the respectable exterior:
And here comes the sentence that has troubled consciences for centuries:
“Go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me.”
And finally the center of everything:
Jesus was not merely recruiting another philanthropist.
The command to sell exposed what prevented this particular man from following Him.
“And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions.”
The Greek describes him as στυγνάσας—stygnasas—a word conveying a darkening, gloomy or downcast response.
But when Eternal Life Himself stood before him, another treasure was already occupying the throne.
This is why reducing the passage to “Jesus hates wealth” misses the point.
But reducing it to “Jesus wasn’t really serious about money” misses the point just as badly.
So does Jesus require every Christian to become materially poor?
Scripture does not present the command to this man as a universal command requiring every believer to liquidate every possession.
We can see this from the broader witness of Scripture.
Jesus interacted with people who possessed material resources without issuing this identical command to each of them.
Zacchaeus provides a particularly revealing comparison.
“Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor…”
“This day is salvation come to this house…”
The point is not that giving away half automatically saves anyone. It does not.
Zacchaeus’ changed relationship with wealth was evidence of something deeper happening in him.
And grace was rearranging the furniture of his heart.
Consider also believers who continued to have homes.
Acts 12:12 describes believers gathered at the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark.
Philemon appears to have had a home large enough for a church to meet there.
Paul instructed wealthy Christians not that they must necessarily dispose of every possession, but:
“Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches…”
He continues by telling them to do good, to be rich in good works, generous, and willing to share.
That would be a strange instruction if Christian conversion universally required wealthy believers immediately to cease possessing wealth.
Job possessed wealth, lost it catastrophically, and later received material restoration.
Joseph of Arimathea is explicitly described in Matthew 27:57 as a rich man and is remembered for providing his own new tomb for Jesus’ burial.
So the biblical conclusion cannot simply be:
Because Scripture gives us something far more uncomfortable:
“How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!”
“Children, how hard is it for them that trust in riches to enter into the kingdom of God!”
“It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God.”
We should not soften that picture unnecessarily.
Jesus is describing impossibility from the human side.
The disciples understood the force of it because they responded:
“With men it is impossible, but not with God: for with God all things are possible.”
There is the Gospel hiding inside the terrifying warning.
Salvation is impossible for you to manufacture.
The religious cannot perform enough for it.
The broken cannot repair themselves enough to obtain it.
Salvation is the work of God.
That is why the story is ultimately much bigger than money.
It is about the horrifying ability of the human heart to stand inches away from Jesus while still clutching something else.
And wealth is particularly dangerous because money can imitate attributes we should ultimately seek in God.
“If everything falls apart, I can save you.”
And suddenly a tool becomes a functional savior.
Scripture does not say money itself is the root of all evil, despite the way the verse is often quoted.
ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
The crucial word is φιλαργυρία — philargyria: love of money.
Money can feed a hungry child.
Money can become an extraordinary servant.
But it makes a terrible god.
And perhaps the most frightening form of greed is the kind we have renamed “normal.”
We compare ourselves with someone richer and conclude we cannot possibly be greedy.
We spend enormous amounts making ourselves comfortable and then hesitate over generosity because we are “trying to be responsible.”
Meanwhile Jesus asks a question beneath all our financial vocabulary:
Maybe you would never bow before a golden statue.
But perhaps you check your balance whenever fear rises.
Maybe you would never verbally deny Christ.
But perhaps obedience becomes negotiable whenever it threatens your lifestyle.
But somewhere inside you there is an asterisk.
And that is precisely where the rich man’s story stops being his story.
Something we instinctively grip tighter when Jesus gets close.
For one person it is money.
For another it is sexual sin.
For another it is a relationship God has clearly told them to leave.
For another it is the desperate need to be admired.
For another it is the secret life nobody at church knows exists.
You can hide an idol underneath Christian vocabulary.
You can call disobedience “waiting on God.”
But when Jesus touches the throne of your heart, excuses eventually run out.
This does not mean Christians should become financially reckless.
Biblical generosity is not an excuse to neglect genuine responsibilities.
Scripture speaks about providing for one’s household. Paul writes in 1 Timothy 5:8 about the seriousness of failing to provide for one’s own.
Scripture condemns oppression of the poor.
Scripture repeatedly reminds God’s people that what they possess ultimately belongs under God’s authority.
Christianity is therefore neither worship of wealth nor worship of poverty.
The question is no longer merely:
“How much am I allowed to keep?”
“Jesus, what do You want me to do with what You have entrusted to me?”
And stewardship can be terrifying because a steward does not ultimately own what passes through his hands.
“For all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee.”
Everything belongs beneath the lordship of Christ.
And this is where we must guard against another distortion.
You cannot buy God’s favor through giving.
You cannot donate yourself into heaven.
You cannot share a Gospel article enough times to erase your sin.
The Gospel would cease to be grace if that were true.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Jesus paid the price you could never pay.
At the cross, Christ did not offer God a percentage.
The sinless Son of God bore sin.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by humanity.
The One through whom all things were made entered our poverty, suffering, shame and death.
This is why Christian generosity is not payment for salvation.
It is a response to salvation.
We do not give so Christ will love us.
We give because in Christ we have encountered a love more valuable than everything we could clutch.
“Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.”
Paul’s context is generosity, but the riches ultimately offered through Christ are far greater than financial prosperity.
The rich young ruler was invited to exchange temporary treasure for eternal treasure.
But he could not release what was in his hands.
And before judging him too quickly…
What would make your face fall if Jesus asked for it?
That answer may reveal more about your spiritual condition than a thousand religious statements.
“Lo, we have left all, and have followed thee.”
Jesus did not pretend sacrifice was meaningless.
He promised that nothing genuinely surrendered for Him and for the Gospel escapes God’s notice.
But Mark’s account also includes two words prosperity preaching often prefers not to emphasize:
Following Christ is not a financial investment strategy.
Jesus is not promising a luxury upgrade for people who donate enough money.
He is calling disciples to Himself.
And eventually that road leads to a cross.
“Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
Maybe Jesus will never tell you to liquidate every possession.
But He does claim something far greater.
Not because He is trying to destroy you.
Because He is rescuing you from spending your life worshiping things that cannot survive your funeral.
One day someone else will live in the house you fought to afford.
Someone else may drive the vehicle you polished.
Someone else will sort through the possessions you protected.
And eventually this world will stop saying your name.
Maybe that is why Jesus said:
“Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven…”
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”
So examine where your treasure goes.
It may reveal where your heart is already traveling.
Perhaps you have spent years appearing spiritually healthy while secretly trusting money more than God.
Perhaps you have been generous only when generosity did not hurt.
Perhaps you have treated Christianity as something added to your lifestyle rather than surrendering your life to Christ.
Perhaps your problem is not wealth at all.
Perhaps Jesus has already shown you the thing you refuse to release.
The story of the rich ruler does not teach that Jesus despises people with idols.
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Christ exposes idols because He loves sinners.
Conviction is not an invitation to hide.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
Grace means your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus entered his house, and a transformed man emerged.
The cross is filled with stories humanity would have written off.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Maybe today the scandal is not public.
Maybe your scandal is simply that Jesus has been receiving the leftovers while something else has been receiving your heart.
“Jesus, show me what I am unwilling to surrender.”
Then do not be surprised when He answers.
Let it be an honest confession that you do not want to walk away from Jesus clutching something that can never save you.
There is no shame in admitting the battle is real.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still transforms people.
Not because saving a post earns anything from God, but because there may come a day when comfort starts whispering louder than Christ and you need to read Mark 10 again.
And think of one person while you are reading this.
The successful friend who has everything except peace.
The believer quietly drowning in materialism.
The person chasing money because poverty once terrified them.
The Christian who loves Jesus but has slowly allowed comfort to become an idol.
The seeker who thinks Christianity is merely about behaving better.

Not as a transaction with God. But if this message faithfully points people toward Christ, sharing it can be one practical way of helping put biblical truth in front of someone who may never walk into a church.

If you genuinely want to glorify God through what you have, ask how your resources, influence, voice, time, and opportunities can serve His purposes. Supporting Christ-centered Gospel work can be one expression of that stewardship—not the price of salvation and never a substitute for obedience, generosity to people in need, faithfulness to your local church, or personal discipleship.
Your share does not save you.
Your comment does not cleanse you.
The rich young ruler arrived asking what he could do to inherit eternal life.
Jesus ultimately revealed what he could not surrender.
And maybe that is the question still echoing across two thousand years.
“How little can I give up and still call myself a Christian?”
“If Jesus is truly worth everything… why am I terrified to place everything in His hands?”
You do not need to become poor merely to prove that you love Jesus.
But you cannot follow Jesus while reserving the right to tell Him:
He is not merely Savior from hell.
And the hands asking you to surrender are scarred hands.
Hands that held nothing back at Calvary.
So if Christ puts His finger on your treasure, your comfort, your secret, your pride, your money, your plans, your reputation, or the thing you cannot imagine living without…
do not walk away from Jesus carrying something you will eventually lose anyway.
